title: FISHER: Gradient-Decoupled Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning for Fine-Grained Aquatic Species Recognition
comment: Submitted for possible publication (13 pages, 11 Figures, 9 Tables)
summary: Fine-grained recognition of aquatic species is challenging due to subtle morphological differences and long-tailed distributions, where ultra-rare species are underrepresented. A natural solution is to jointly model segmentation, morphological traits, and species classification within a multi-task learning (MTL) framework. However, existing MTL methods suffer from negative transfer caused by gradient conflicts between low-level dense tasks and high-level classification objectives, degrading fine-grained representations. To address this limitation, we identify gradient interference across hierarchical tasks as a fundamental bottleneck and propose FISHER, a gradient-decoupled hierarchical multi-task learning framework. FISHER aligns optimization with the biological hierarchy of aquatic species by enforcing a unidirectional information flow from segmentation to trait prediction and finally to species classification, while explicitly decoupling gradients across task boundaries. This design prevents high-level objectives from corrupting low-level morphological representations, effectively mitigating negative transfer while preserving the benefits of shared supervision. Furthermore, we introduce a prototype-based segmentation head with orthogonality regularization to encourage disentangled anatomical representations, and employ homoscedastic uncertainty weighting to dynamically balance task contributions during training. Our analysis shows that robust trait representations serve as a critical bridge for transferring knowledge to ultra-rare species. Extensive experiments on the Fish-Vista benchmark demonstrate that FISHER achieves 97.7% mAP for unseen trait identification and improves ultra-rare species classification accuracy by 13.4% over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of gradient-decoupled hierarchical learning for long-tailed biodiversity recognition.

AI.tldr: FISHER is a gradient-decoupled hierarchical multi-task learning framework that mitigates negative transfer in fine-grained aquatic species recognition by enforcing unidirectional information flow from segmentation to trait prediction to classification, achieving 97.7% mAP for unseen traits and 13.4% improvement in ultra-rare species classification.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained aquatic species recognition is challenging due to subtle morphological differences and long-tailed distributions with underrepresented ultra-rare species. Existing MTL methods suffer from negative transfer caused by gradient conflicts between low-level dense tasks and high-level classification objectives, degrading fine-grained representations.
AI.method: FISHER proposes a gradient-decoupled hierarchical MTL framework with: (1) unidirectional information flow from segmentation → trait prediction → species classification; (2) explicit gradient decoupling across task boundaries; (3) a prototype-based segmentation head with orthogonality regularization for disentangled anatomical representations; (4) homoscedastic uncertainty weighting for dynamic task balancing.
AI.result: On Fish-Vista benchmark: 97.7% mAP for unseen trait identification; 13.4% improvement in ultra-rare species classification accuracy over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Robust trait representations serve as a critical bridge for transferring knowledge to ultra-rare species, and gradient-decoupled hierarchical learning is effective for long-tailed biodiversity recognition.

title: Auditing pretraining contamination in single-cell foundation model benchmarks
summary: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) such as Geneformer, scGPT, and Universal Cell Embeddings (UCE) are pretrained on tens of millions of cells drawn from public repositories. The same repositories underlie widely used integration benchmarks, creating an unmeasured risk that zero-shot benchmark performance reflects pretraining exposure rather than genuine generalization. We introduce \textbf{scContam}, a per-cell audit framework that combines a MinHash-based gene-set fingerprint signal against the explicit pretraining corpus with a loss-based membership inference attack (MIA-scFM). Applied to four scIB benchmarks and three scFMs, we find that two of the most-cited benchmarks, PBMC 3k and the CELLxGENE human pancreatic islet atlas, contain extensive pretraining-overlap evidence ($80.4\%$ and $77.0\%$ of cells with fingerprint $p < 0.05$ against Genecorpus-30M), whereas the post-cutoff datasets AIDA v2 and Tahoe-100M show no overlap evidence ($0\%$). A controlled re-pretraining experiment establishes that MIA-scFM AUROC scales monotonically with the model's capacity-to-data ratio (AUROC $0.494 \to 0.690 \to 0.881$ across properly-regularized, mildly-overfit, and aggressively-overfit regimes), demonstrating that production scFMs resist instance-level memorization but distributional contamination must be detected separately. A donor-matched, within-cell-type analysis with three architectures shows that contaminated cells embed measurably more tightly than donor-matched clean cells (permutation $p = 0.030, 0.014, < 0.002$, respectively), with a perfectly null AIDA negative control. Pretraining audits are tractable and should accompany scFM benchmark reporting.

AI.tldr: Introduces scContam, an audit framework detecting pretraining overlap in single-cell foundation models. Finds extensive contamination in two popular benchmarks (PBMC 3k, CELLxGENE pancreas) while post-cutoff datasets show no overlap. Demonstrates that contamination distorts embeddings even when instance-level memorization is absent.
AI.motivation: Public single-cell repositories are used for both pretraining scFMs and integration benchmarks, creating an unmeasured risk that zero-shot benchmark performance reflects pretraining data exposure rather than genuine generalization.
AI.method: scContam audit framework combining MinHash-based gene-set fingerprint detection against the pretraining corpus with a loss-based membership inference attack (MIA-scFM). Applied to four scIB benchmarks and three scFMs. Includes controlled re-pretraining experiments and donor-matched within-cell-type analyses.
AI.result: PBMC 3k (80.4%) and CELLxGENE pancreas (77.0%) show extensive pretraining overlap; AIDA v2 and Tahoe-100M show 0% overlap. MIA-scFM AUROC scales with overfitting (0.494→0.690→0.881). Contaminated cells embed more tightly than clean cells across three architectures.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining audits are tractable and should be standard practice in scFM benchmark reporting.

title: Foundation-model-guided radiogenomic discovery linking cancer genomes to cancer scans
summary: The function of many genes is still unknown, and conventional driver-discovery methods, which rely on how frequently a gene is mutated, cannot assess genes that are only rarely affected. Here we pair Evo~2-based genome analysis with routine clinical imaging to identify gene--phenotype associations at genome-wide scale. For every somatic mutation across three TCGA cohorts (cRCC=clear cell renal cell carcinoma, HCC=hepatocellular carcinoma, and BC=breast cancer; $n = 340$ total), Evo~2 predicts a severity score, with no task-specific training. Per-gene severity summaries are then correlated with radiomic features extracted from paired tumor segmentations, controlling for total mutation burden. In TCGA-cRCC ($n = 162$), this sweep recovers established renal-cancer drivers and identifies 46 additional genes reaching false discovery rate (FDR) significance absent from curated cancer-gene panels, several of which are Mendelian ciliopathy and cytoskeletal-disease genes. These results demonstrate that pairing a genomic language model with widely available clinical imaging can serve as a hypothesis-free discovery tool for gene--imaging associations invisible to conventional approaches.

AI.tldr: Evo~2, a genomic language model, pairs genome analysis with clinical imaging to discover gene-phenotype associations for rarely mutated genes. Applied to three TCGA cohorts, it recovers known drivers and identifies 46 new FDR-significant genes (including Mendelian disease genes) invisible to conventional frequency-based methods.
AI.motivation: Many genes have unknown functions, and conventional driver-discovery methods fail to assess rarely mutated genes, leaving a gap in understanding genotype-phenotype relationships.
AI.method: Evo~2 predicts severity scores for somatic mutations across TCGA cohorts (cRCC, HCC, BC; n=340) without task-specific training. Per-gene severity summaries are correlated with radiomic features from tumor segmentations, controlling for total mutation burden.
AI.result: In TCGA-cRCC (n=162), the method recovers established renal-cancer drivers and identifies 46 additional FDR-significant genes absent from curated cancer-gene panels, including Mendelian ciliopathy and cytoskeletal-disease genes.
AI.conclusion: Pairing a genomic language model with routine clinical imaging provides a hypothesis-free discovery tool for gene-imaging associations invisible to conventional frequency-based approaches.

title: Spectral theory for population density dynamics of spiking neurons with refractoriness
summary: Incorporating an absolute refractory period into the population density approach for spiking neurons remains an open problem, despite evidence that refractoriness can strongly affect nonlinear transfer functions and network stability. We develop a rigorous operator-theoretic framework for neuronal population dynamics with a finite refractory time by augmenting the state space to include refractory history and formulating the problem as a non-self-adjoint boundary eigenvalue problem for the Fokker-Planck operator. This yields a complete spectral characterization of the generator, proves dissipativity and the existence of a contraction semigroup, and identifies defective eigenvalues as exceptional points where oscillatory modes emerge from coalescing relaxational modes. Within the framework of linear response theory, we also derive an exact transfer function that accounts for boundary conditions modulated by external input, correcting previous heuristic derivations and revealing additional threshold-noise contributions. Using this transfer function under a mean-field approximation, we further show that refractoriness in populations of interacting neurons can facilitate the onset of limit cycles, that is, stable oscillations in the firing rate. These results provide a rigorous foundation for spectral decomposition methods in computational neuroscience, opening the way to their further rigorous mathematical analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a rigorous operator-theoretic framework for neuronal population dynamics with absolute refractory periods by augmenting the state space and formulating a non-self-adjoint boundary eigenvalue problem for the Fokker-Planck operator, deriving exact transfer functions and showing refractoriness can facilitate oscillatory firing patterns.
AI.motivation: Incorporating absolute refractory periods into population density approaches for spiking neurons has remained an open problem, despite evidence that refractoriness strongly affects nonlinear transfer functions and network stability.
AI.method: The authors develop an operator-theoretic framework by augmenting the state space to include refractory history, formulating a non-self-adjoint boundary eigenvalue problem for the Fokker-Planck operator, and deriving an exact transfer function via linear response theory.
AI.result: Complete spectral characterization of the generator is achieved, proving dissipativity and existence of a contraction semigroup. Defective eigenvalues are identified as exceptional points where oscillatory modes emerge. The exact transfer function corrects previous heuristic derivations and reveals additional threshold-noise contributions.
AI.conclusion: Refractoriness in interacting neuronal populations can facilitate the onset of limit cycles (stable oscillations in firing rate), and the framework provides a rigorous foundation for spectral decomposition methods in computational neuroscience.

title: Transition-Related Potentials as Markers of Narrative Comprehension in Continuous EEG
summary: Harnessing the potential of electroencephalography (EEG) for brain research is fundamentally limited by intrinsic noise and the diffuse projection of brain-generated activity over the scalp. The standard event-related potential (ERP) paradigm addresses this limitation by relying on repeated independent trials, albeit at the cost of moving away from naturalistic experimental conditions. As a more naturalistic alternative, we collected continuous EEG while participants watched short films and extracted potentials aligned to sharp cinematic transitions (cuts). We demonstrate that such transition-related potentials (TRPs) exhibit canonical ERP-like temporal structure associated with significant information processing. By comparing coherent films with scene-scrambled versions containing matched post-cut sensory input, we find that these responses are systematically shaped by narrative context. We then show that the cut-related EEG signature can be recovered directly from group-averaged continuous recordings with a compact deep neural network (DNN). The detector generalized across films and subject groups, and the resulting TRPs reproduced the main context-dependent effects observed for manually annotated cuts. These results indicate that narrative context leaves a measurable signature in EEG responses, that this signature can be detected directly in continuous recordings, and that such detections provide a semi-automated framework for analyzing how viewers process and understand film narratives. We propose that the method outlined here can be adapted to parse EEG responses to other forms of continuous stimulation, providing a general tool for probing experimental conditions that are closer to natural human experience.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that EEG responses to film cuts (transition-related potentials, TRPs) exhibit ERP-like temporal structure shaped by narrative context, and these signals can be detected automatically from continuous recordings using a deep neural network, offering a semi-automated framework for studying naturalistic brain processing.
AI.motivation: Traditional ERP paradigms rely on repeated independent trials, which limits their applicability to naturalistic conditions. The authors aim to study brain responses during continuous, naturalistic stimuli (films) while still recovering meaningful neural signals.
AI.method: Participants watched short films during continuous EEG recording. The authors extracted potentials aligned to cinematic cuts (TRPs), compared coherent vs. scene-scrambled films to isolate narrative context effects, and used a compact deep neural network to detect cut-related EEG signatures from group-averaged continuous recordings.
AI.result: TRPs exhibit canonical ERP-like temporal structure shaped by narrative context. The DNN detector generalized across films and subject groups, reproducing context-dependent effects observed from manually annotated cuts.
AI.conclusion: Narrative context leaves measurable signatures in EEG responses that can be detected automatically in continuous recordings, providing a semi-automated framework for analyzing naturalistic stimuli processing, with potential generalization to other continuous stimulation paradigms.

title: Analyzing \b{eta}-Lactamase Evolution from the Principle of Least Action Perspective
summary: Protein sequences change over time due to the accumulation of mutations in the genes that encode them. Nonetheless, accurately identifying the most probable evolutionary pathways and more efficient trajectories between an ancestral and a derived sequence remains a challenge. This difficulty stems from a limited understanding of the critical factors that drive the evolutionary process. This study aims to address this issue by validating a newly proposed mechanistic model (grounded on the principle of least action) for analyzing protein evolution, using beta-lactamase as an empirically characterized evolutionary model. The initial findings indicate that, after accounting for how mutations and the context-dependent interactions between them (epistasis) affect protein stability and, hence, the kinetics of protein folding, a resort to the principle of least action allows us to simultaneously identify the most probable pathways and the most efficient trajectories swiftly and accurately. These findings also suggest that the most probable evolutionary protein pathways are the ones that exhibit the most efficient trajectories. All in all, our study addresses several unanswered questions regarding the main factors that govern how protein evolves at the molecular level (under constant selection pressure) and outlines directions for future research in key fields such as directed evolution and ancestral sequence reconstruction.

AI.tldr: This paper validates a principle-of-least-action-based mechanistic model for protein evolution using beta-lactamase, showing that accounting for mutation effects and epistasis on protein stability and folding kinetics allows simultaneous identification of the most probable and most efficient evolutionary pathways.
AI.motivation: Accurately identifying the most probable evolutionary pathways and efficient trajectories between ancestral and derived protein sequences remains challenging due to limited understanding of critical factors driving the evolutionary process.
AI.method: The authors validate a mechanistic model grounded in the principle of least action, incorporating mutation effects and context-dependent epistasis on protein stability and folding kinetics, using beta-lactamase as an empirical evolutionary model.
AI.result: The model simultaneously and accurately identifies both the most probable pathways and the most efficient trajectories; most probable pathways correspond to the most efficient ones.
AI.conclusion: The study addresses unanswered questions about molecular-level protein evolution under constant selection pressure and outlines future research directions in directed evolution and ancestral sequence reconstruction.

title: A Bayesian-optimization framework coupling a multiphase PDE tumor model to efficiently design combination therapy schedules
summary: Designing combination cancer therapies requires choosing not only which agents to combine but also their relative doses and timing decisions that critically shape the trade-off between efficacy and toxicity. High-fidelity mechanistic models of tumor growth, formulated as systems of coupled PDEs, can in principle resolve how these scheduling choices interact with the tumor microenvironment, but each evaluation is computationally expensive, rendering brute-force exploration of the design space intractable. We present a Bayesian Optimization framework that treats a multiphase, vascularized, two-dimensional PDE tumor simulator as a black box and uses a Gaussian-process surrogate to find schedules that maximize therapeutic outcomes within a small budget of expensive simulations. We orchestrate the COMSOL Multiphysics solver from Python, producing a fully automated optimization loop in which a single simulation of ~650 days of tumor evolution requires roughly 80 hours of wall time. The framework is applied to three clinically relevant scenarios: (i) a two-agent regimen (docetaxel + bevacizumab), (ii) a three-agent regimen (docetaxel + bevacizumab + radiation) under reduced and full intensity, and (iii) a single-agent dose-fractionation problem in which efficacy is balanced against healthy-tissue toxicity through a weighted multi-objective formulation. The BO loop converges to clinically plausible optima with one to two orders of magnitude fewer simulations than an equivalent grid search, identifies docetaxel-induced radiosensitization as a decisive factor in the triple-therapy optimum, and recovers a fractionation regime consistent with clinical protocols when both efficacy and toxicity are considered. The framework is agnostic to the specifics of the underlying PDE model and provides a transferable methodology for design optimization of expensive engineered or biological simulators.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian Optimization framework efficiently identifies optimal combination cancer therapy schedules (dose, timing) by treating an expensive PDE tumor simulator as a black box, achieving clinically plausible optima with 1-2 orders of magnitude fewer simulations than grid search.
AI.motivation: Designing combination cancer therapies requires optimizing not just which agents but also their doses and timing, which critically affects efficacy-toxicity trade-offs. High-fidelity PDE models can capture these interactions but are computationally prohibitive for brute-force exploration.
AI.method: Bayesian Optimization with a Gaussian-process surrogate treats a multiphase, vascularized 2D PDE tumor simulator (COMSOL, automated from Python) as a black box to find optimal schedules within a small simulation budget.
AI.result: BO converges to clinically plausible optima with 1-2 orders fewer simulations than grid search; identifies docetaxel-induced radiosensitization as decisive in triple therapy; recovers clinically consistent fractionation regimes under multi-objective efficacy-toxicity trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: The framework is agnostic to the underlying PDE model and provides a transferable methodology for design optimization of expensive biological or engineered simulators.

title: Evolutionary Le Chatelier's Principle: Phenotypic Plasticity and Genetic Assimilation via Timescale Separation in the Price Equation
summary: Phenotypic plasticity and genetic assimilation play key roles in adaptive evolution, yet their underlying mechanism has lacked a unified physical description. A major theoretical difficulty lies in the fundamental difference in timescales, as phenotypic plasticity occurs rapidly within a generation whereas genetic changes accumulate slowly across generations. Here, we formalize these processes by bridging the continuous-time Price equation, a foundational equation of evolutionary dynamics, with the physical concept of timescale separation. A sudden environmental change induces a fast plastic displacement of the phenotype relative to the slow genotypic variable. Through genotype--phenotype coupling, this displacement generates an internal genetic stress. We demonstrate that genetic assimilation is a dynamical relaxation process in which the genotype evolves to resolve this self-generated stress. These evolutionary dynamics mathematically realize Le Chatelier's principle, where the slow genetic response naturally amplifies the initial plastic shift in the same direction. The theory predicts that a weaker restoring force, which can manifest as larger clonal phenotypic fluctuations, requires a longer evolutionary timescale for assimilation. In the ideal limit of cost-free, perfectly adaptive plasticity, the relaxation time diverges, so assimilation effectively stalls. This formulation provides a macroscopic physical mechanism for genetic assimilation, offering a universal response law for evolutionary systems in which rapid phenotypic responses precede slower genetic change.

AI.tldr: The paper bridges the Price equation with timescale separation to show that genetic assimilation is a relaxation process resolving internal genetic stress, following Le Chatelier's principle, where weaker restoring forces slow assimilation and perfect plasticity stalls it entirely.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified physical description of phenotypic plasticity and genetic assimilation, overcoming the theoretical difficulty of their vastly different timescales (fast plastic vs. slow genetic changes).
AI.method: Bridges the continuous-time Price equation with the physical concept of timescale separation to formalize the interaction between fast plastic responses and slow genetic evolution.
AI.result: Genetic assimilation is a relaxation process resolving self-generated genetic stress; weaker restoring forces (larger clonal fluctuations) slow assimilation, and perfect adaptive plasticity causes assimilation to stall.
AI.conclusion: The theory provides a universal response law (Le Chatelier's principle) for evolutionary systems where rapid phenotypic responses precede slower genetic changes.

title: From Berg-Purcell precision bounds to clock-limited information capacity
summary: Physical limits to chemical sensing are traditionally expressed as Berg-Purcell bounds on estimation accuracy. Whether these bounds also limit the total amount of information a molecular receptor can transmit has remained unclear, despite the fact that cellular signaling performance is naturally quantified in bits rather than precision alone. Here we derive an explicit link between Berg-Purcell-type sensing limits and the information capacity of a single two-state receptor, yielding a compact expression that separates contributions from concentration range, receptor copy number, and averaging time. We show that, in the ideal fixed-time occupancy model, diffusion-limited sampling alone does not define a finite global information bound: with a perfectly specified integration window and unbounded input range, information capacity grows without bound with dynamic range, albeit slowly. A finite saturation arises when time integration is treated as an explicit physical resource. Finite timing precision yields a clock-limited bound on information capacity, and in the high-occupancy regime information transmission crosses over from diffusion-limited to clock-limited behavior. Together, these results establish a receptor-level information bound in bits that is finite once constraints on timing precision are taken into account.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a link between Berg-Purcell sensing limits and information capacity of a two-state receptor, showing that diffusion alone doesn't bound information—finite timing precision does.
AI.motivation: To determine whether classical Berg-Purcell bounds on estimation accuracy also constrain the total information (in bits) that a molecular receptor can transmit, which was previously unclear.
AI.method: Derives an explicit connection between Berg-Purcell-type limits and information capacity of a single two-state receptor, analyzing contributions from concentration range, receptor copy number, and averaging time.
AI.result: Diffusion-limited sampling alone does not bound information capacity; unbounded dynamic range allows unbounded information. Finite timing precision yields a clock-limited bound, with crossover from diffusion-limited to clock-limited behavior in high-occupancy regime.
AI.conclusion: Receptor-level information bounds in bits become finite only when timing precision constraints are taken into account.

title: Local intercellular coupling is sufficient for long-range calcium signaling
summary: Long-range intercellular calcium (Ca2+) signaling coordinates biological processes ranging from fertilization to contraction and cell death. The classical model attributes this long-range propagation to rapid diffusion of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) through gap junctions. However, recent evidence that IP3 diffuses far more slowly than previously believed, and that Ca2+ oscillations persist even when gap junctions are disassembled, indicates that an alternative mechanism must sustain long-range communication. Here we develop a computational model showing that local coupling between neighboring cells is sufficient to generate and propagate regenerative Ca2+ oscillations across a cell population without fast molecular diffusion. Each cell is treated as an oscillator whose intrinsic frequency is set by its local IP3 concentration through an IP3-dependent refractory period, and neighboring cells are coupled using a Kuramoto nearest-neighbor framework. In a dual-stiffness regime, cells on a stiff extracellular matrix entrain their soft-matrix neighbors, producing an offset traveling wave of Ca2+ release. This reproduces the finite spatial range of influence (~8 cell lengths) observed experimentally. Our findings propose a diffusion-independent paradigm for calcium signaling in which local intercellular coupling drives long-range communication, offering insight into how localized ECM stiffening in asthma and fibrosis may produce systemic effects.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a diffusion-independent model for long-range calcium signaling, showing that local coupling between neighboring cells can generate and propagate regenerative Ca2+ oscillations across cell populations without requiring fast molecular diffusion of IP3.
AI.motivation: To resolve the paradox that IP3 diffuses too slowly to explain long-range Ca2+ signaling, and that Ca2+ oscillations persist without gap junctions, suggesting an alternative mechanism is needed.
AI.method: A computational model where each cell is an oscillator with IP3-dependent refractory period, coupled via Kuramoto nearest-neighbor framework in a dual-stiffness regime (stiff vs. soft ECM).
AI.result: Cells on stiff ECM entrain soft-matrix neighbors, producing offset traveling waves of Ca2+ release with a finite spatial influence (~8 cell lengths), matching experimental observations.
AI.conclusion: Long-range Ca2+ signaling can be driven by local intercellular coupling without fast diffusion, explaining how localized ECM stiffening in diseases like asthma and fibrosis could produce systemic effects.

title: Magnetosensitivity of amphibian morphological pigmentation is light- and eye-dependent and consistent with the radical pair mechanism
summary: Weak magnetic fields influence a wide range of biological processes, yet the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. The radical pair mechanism (RPM), which involves quantum spin dynamics, is a leading hypothesis. Here we show that weak magnetic fields modulate morphological pigmentation -- specifically, the number of perioptic melanophores -- in Xenopus laevis tadpoles in a field-strength-dependent manner. The response is light- and eye-dependent. The observed field-strength dependence is quantitatively consistent with a radical pair model. These properties are reminiscent of the light-dependent magnetoreception that is thought to operate in migratory birds, and establish amphibian pigmentation as a tractable vertebrate system for the study of radical-pair quantum biology.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that weak magnetic fields affect melanophore numbers in Xenopus laevis tadpoles in a field-strength-dependent manner, consistent with the radical pair mechanism, establishing a new vertebrate model for quantum biology.
AI.motivation: Weak magnetic fields influence biological processes but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. The radical pair mechanism (RPM) is a leading hypothesis that needs experimental validation in vertebrate systems.
AI.method: The researchers exposed Xenopus laevis tadpoles to weak magnetic fields of varying strengths and quantified morphological pigmentation changes (specifically perioptic melanophore numbers). They also tested light- and eye-dependence of the response and compared observed field-strength dependence with a radical pair model.
AI.result: Weak magnetic fields modulate pigmentation in a field-strength-dependent manner. The response requires light and eyes. The observed field-strength dependence quantitatively matches predictions from a radical pair model.
AI.conclusion: The findings are reminiscent of light-dependent magnetoreception in migratory birds, and establish amphibian pigmentation as a tractable vertebrate system for studying radical-pair quantum biology.

title: SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction
summary: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

AI.tldr: SenCos-GEM is a molecular representation learning framework that uses physics-guided geometric consistency (law of cosines) and SENet-based feature modulation to improve molecular property prediction, achieving state-of-the-art results on FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing SSL methods for molecular representation lack explicit physical constraints, are susceptible to geometric noise from coarse force fields, and overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, leading to catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer.
AI.method: SenCos-GEM employs (1) a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines for high-fidelity 3D spatial priors, (2) lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules as task-specific adapters, and (3) a dual-modulation prediction head combining FiLM and SENet for dynamic feature recalibration.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on MoleculeNet benchmarks, with relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE) on FreeSolv, 5.3% (RMSE) on Lipophilicity, and 8.2% (MAE) on QM9, and demonstrates superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and conformational perturbations.
AI.conclusion: SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction by combining explicit physical constraints with dynamic feature modulation.

title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation for Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
summary: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD), an extension of Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI), has emerged as a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for computing molecular ground state energies. By leveraging quantum sampling instead of variational optimization, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and enables direct reconstruction of correlated electronic wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery techniques primarily enforce symmetry constraints without guaranteeing optimal selection of the most physically relevant configurations, often leading to unnecessarily large subspaces and increased classical diagonalization costs. In this work, we introduce a machine-learned compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), termed QSCI-RBM, and integrate it within the Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) framework. The RBM is trained on quantum-sampled configurations to learn the underlying probability distribution of dominant determinants, enabling the targeted generation of high-probability configurations. We apply this framework to the simulation of a protein-ligand complex involving the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease ($M^{\text{pro}}$). Our results demonstrate that DMET-QSCI-RBM achieves energies within the chemical accuracy threshold by accessing only approximately 4% of the configuration subspace. In contrast, standard DMET-SQD simulations failed to reach chemical accuracy while accessing up to 20% of the subspace, even as the chemical potential itself nearly converged. These findings highlight that RBM-assisted configuration generation produces significantly more compact subspaces while preserving physical accuracy, thereby reducing classical computational overhead and enabling the scalable quantum embedding simulation of complex biological systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces QSCI-RBM, a machine-learned protocol using Restricted Boltzmann Machines to generate compact configuration subspaces for quantum diagonalization, achieving chemical accuracy on a SARS-CoV-2 protein-ligand complex using only ~4% of the configuration subspace, compared to standard SQD methods that failed even at 20%.
AI.motivation: Existing configuration recovery techniques in QSCI/SQD primarily enforce symmetry constraints without guaranteeing optimal selection of physically relevant configurations, leading to unnecessarily large subspaces and increased classical diagonalization costs.
AI.method: Integrates a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) trained on quantum-sampled configurations to learn the probability distribution of dominant determinants, enabling targeted generation of high-probability configurations, embedded within the Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) framework.
AI.result: DMET-QSCI-RBM achieves chemical accuracy using only ~4% of the configuration subspace, while standard DMET-SQD fails to reach chemical accuracy even when accessing up to 20% of the subspace.
AI.conclusion: RBM-assisted configuration generation produces significantly more compact subspaces while preserving physical accuracy, reducing classical computational overhead and enabling scalable quantum embedding simulation of complex biological systems.

title: Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents
summary: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether Integrated Information Decomposition (Φr) tracks learning in active inference agents, finding that aggregate Φr is largely architectural and decreases with training, while meaningful learning effects only appear at the atom-compositional level where decoupling flips sign and downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustment.
AI.motivation: To investigate how Integrated Information Decomposition (Φr) relates to reward-free predictive organization in active inference agents, specifically testing whether Φr tracks learned integration in the absence of reward signals.
AI.method: An active inference agent with a hierarchical architecture separating fast perception latent z from slow global latent g (driven by prediction error, decoupled from policy gradients) is tested in a reward-free regime-switching protocol. Φr is analyzed at both aggregate and atom-compositional levels.
AI.result: Φr concentrates in the slow global latent g; aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. At the atom-compositional level, decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustment.
AI.conclusion: The slow global latent g is the architectural locus of Φr-relevant temporal organization in active inference agents. Scalar Φr should not be read as a direct index of learned integration, as the substantive learning effects are only visible at finer-grained compositional analysis.

title: Importance-Sampling Estimation of Gaussian Molecular Shape Overlap: Exact Union Volumes and Confidence-Bounded Virtual Screening
summary: Gaussian descriptions of molecular shape underpin 3D shape-based virtual screening, but existing methods evaluate Gaussian overlap analytically. The widely used first-order approximation is fast but systematically overestimates overlap, whereas the exact molecular volume requires a combinatorial inclusion-exclusion expansion. We introduce the first stochastic estimator of Gaussian shape overlap: an unbiased Monte Carlo method that importance-samples directly from a molecule's Gaussian mixture. The estimator reproduces analytic overlap without bias and extends to the exact union volume of all inclusion-exclusion orders with O(N) cost per sample. On drug-like molecules, the union estimator matches high-resolution grid quadrature with a mean relative error of 0.07 percent, while the first-order approximation overestimates the true union volume by 3.4x on average. The estimator provides analytic standard errors, enabling confidence-bounded screening that reduces sampling by 94 percent while preserving ranking. Implemented in JAX, it is fully differentiable and supports gradient-based rigid alignment on CPU, GPU, and TPU. On the DUD-E and LIT-PCBA benchmarks, the method achieves shape-only enrichment comparable to existing single-conformer approaches while additionally providing unbiased absolute volumes and uncertainty estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Monte Carlo method for unbiased estimation of Gaussian molecular shape overlap, enabling exact union volume computation with O(N) cost, confidence-bounded screening that reduces sampling by 94%, and GPU-accelerated differentiable shape alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing Gaussian shape overlap methods either use a fast but systematically overestimating first-order approximation or require a combinatorial inclusion-exclusion expansion for exact volume. A stochastic estimator that is both unbiased and computationally efficient is needed.
AI.method: An unbiased Monte Carlo estimator that importance-samples from a molecule's Gaussian mixture, extending to exact union volume across all inclusion-exclusion orders with O(N) cost per sample, implemented in JAX for differentiation and hardware acceleration.
AI.result: Matches grid quadrature with 0.07% mean relative error for union volume; first-order approximation overestimates by 3.4x; confidence-bounded screening reduces sampling by 94% while preserving ranking; achieves competitive shape-only enrichment on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed stochastic estimator provides unbiased absolute volumes, uncertainty estimates, and gradient-based alignment, combining accuracy and efficiency in a fully differentiable framework suitable for modern hardware.

title: Fluctuation impossibility results for stochastic burst networks
summary:
Stochastic reaction networks often involve components at low copy number, where individual production and degradation events generate substantial fluctuations. Yan et al.\ conjectured in 2019 that for networks with linear degradation and arbitrary cross-regulatory production rates, feedback cannot suppress the stationary fluctuations for each component below the fluctuations of its constant-rate counterpart. Their formulation allows random burst sizes $K_i$: the unit-birth case has $K_i\equiv1$, the biologically important burst model takes $K_i$ to be geometrically distributed, but more general positive integer-valued burst laws are also permitted.
  The conjecture was recently proved for unit births, $K_i\equiv1$. We show here that the conjecture is \textit{false in general} by constructing a two-component network with bounded production rates and burst sizes in $\{1,2\}$ for which both stationary Fano factors lie below their common constant-rate baseline. We then prove the conjecture for positive geometric bursts, the canonical burst model in stochastic gene expression. For arbitrary regulatory architecture and nonlinear cross-regulatory production rates, we prove an exact weighted tradeoff that rules out simultaneous suppression of every component below its geometric-burst baseline. We also prove a complementary structural impossibility result for arbitrary positive integer-valued burst laws with finite second moments: if the activating and inhibiting interactions have a globally consistent sign structure, in the sense that every cycle of the regulatory interaction graph contains an even number of negative interactions, then every component individually satisfies $F_{X_i}\ge B_i$, where $F_{X_i}$ is its stationary Fano factor and $B_i$ is its constant-rate burst baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper disproves a 2019 conjecture about stochastic reaction networks for general burst distributions by constructing a counterexample, but proves it holds for geometrically distributed bursts, and establishes weighted tradeoffs and structural impossibility results for other burst distributions.
AI.motivation: To resolve a 2019 conjecture by Yan et al. about whether feedback can suppress stationary fluctuations below constant-rate baselines in stochastic reaction networks with linear degradation and arbitrary cross-regulatory production rates, considering various burst size distributions.
AI.method: Construction of a two-component counterexample network with bounded production rates and burst sizes in {1,2}; analytical proofs for geometric bursts using weighted tradeoffs; structural analysis based on regulatory interaction graph cycle parity.
AI.result: The conjecture is false in general (counterexample found), but true for positive geometric bursts. An exact weighted tradeoff rules out simultaneous suppression for geometric bursts. For arbitrary positive integer-valued bursts with finite second moments, if every cycle in the regulatory graph has an even number of negative interactions, then each component's Fano factor is at least its burst baseline.
AI.conclusion: The Yan et al. conjecture holds for the canonical geometric burst model in stochastic gene expression but fails for more general burst distributions; structural constraints on regulatory interaction graphs can still guarantee the bound for arbitrary burst laws.

title: HierarchicalDAEW: Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted Graph Convolution with Evidential Uncertainty for Multi-Section Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from H&E Histology
summary: Spatial transcriptomics assays remain costly and technically demanding, restricting transcriptome-wide profiling to specialist settings and preventing routine clinical deployment. Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology could close this gap, yet current methods largely ignore the underlying tissue architecture and rarely quantify how their predictions can be trusted. We introduce HierarchicalDAEW, a dual-graph architecture that addresses both gaps. On the spot graph, a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, allowing the model to treat tissue heterogeneity as an explicit structural signal rather than an implicit one. A second gene-level graph then fuses protein-protein interaction priors from STRING-DB with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from a landmark gene set to a broader gene panel. Reliability is handled through evidential uncertainty estimation, which produces far better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout under identical conditions. Across six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains that hold up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations further confirm that both the domain-aware edge typing and the hierarchical depth are necessary to this improvement, and calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

AI.tldr: HierarchicalDAEW introduces a dual-graph architecture with domain-aware edge weighting and evidential uncertainty estimation to predict spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple tissue types while providing calibrated confidence measures.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is costly and technically demanding, preventing routine clinical deployment. Current prediction methods from H&E histology largely ignore underlying tissue architecture and lack reliable uncertainty quantification for their predictions.
AI.method: A dual-graph architecture: (1) a spot graph with Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator handling inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges from Leiden clustering; (2) a gene-level graph fusing STRING-DB priors with tissue-specific co-expression via attention gating. Evidential uncertainty estimation is used for calibrated confidence intervals.
AI.result: Across six human Visium sections (breast, colorectal, prostate, cerebellar tissue) and against thirteen baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains holding under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls.
AI.conclusion: Domain-aware edge typing and hierarchical depth are both necessary for improvement. Calibrated uncertainty estimates enable identification of low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

title: A Kuramoto phase model to explore the synchronisation of a network of circadian clocks
summary: We propose a model of the circadian clock in a population of cells based on a network of oscillators, derived from the Kuramoto model. The coupling between oscillators is described by a global interaction term but we introduce a phase-dependent coupling mechanism, such that oscillators interact only within a specific interval of the cycle corresponding to a specific stage of the circadian cycle. We analytically demonstrate that this modified system achieves complete asymptotic phase synchronisation, provided specific conditions on the initial phase distribution and the coupling window length are met. To bridge this theoretical framework with experimental observations, we introduce a signal processing procedure based on wavelet decomposition to extract quantitative oscillatory features from Per2::luciferase reporter traces. We then calibrate the model against datasets from both wild type and Cry2 knockout hepatocyte spheroids using a two-step quasi-Monte Carlo filtering algorithm. The comparative analysis reveals significant phenotypic divergence, showing that the Cry2KO condition alters the identifiability landscape of the model's parameters and introduces new compensatory mechanisms that confound the initial population heterogeneity with long-term macroscopic signal decay.

AI.tldr: A Kuramoto-based circadian clock model with phase-dependent coupling is proposed, proven to synchronize under certain conditions, calibrated using wavelet-based signal processing of Per2::luciferase data, and applied to compare wild-type vs. Cry2 knockout hepatocyte spheroids, revealing altered parameter identifiability and compensatory mechanisms in the knockout condition.
AI.motivation: To bridge theoretical oscillator models with real circadian clock data, particularly understanding how coupling mechanisms and genetic perturbations (like Cry2 knockout) affect synchronization dynamics in cell populations.
AI.method: (1) Kuramoto model variant with phase-dependent coupling (interaction only within a specific circadian window). (2) Analytical proof of complete asymptotic synchronisation under initial phase distribution and window length conditions. (3) Wavelet decomposition-based signal processing for extracting oscillatory features from Per2::luciferase traces. (4) Two-step quasi-Monte Carlo filtering algorithm for model calibration against wild-type and Cry2KO hepatocyte spheroid data.
AI.result: The modified Kuramoto model achieves complete asymptotic phase synchronisation under specific conditions. Cry2KO condition significantly alters the identifiability landscape of model parameters and introduces compensatory mechanisms that confound initial population heterogeneity with long-term macroscopic signal decay.
AI.conclusion: Phase-dependent coupling is a key feature for modeling circadian clocks, and Cry2 knockout disrupts parameter identifiability, suggesting new compensatory dynamics that need to be accounted for in circadian rhythm models.

title: Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling
comment: Accepted to Graph Foundation Models workshop at ICML '26. Contains 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

AI.tldr: EnsembleEGNN is a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes multiple conformers per molecule using shared EGNN layers and Set Attention Block pooling, pretrained on cyclic peptide ensembles, achieving superior property prediction (R²=0.477) compared to a sequence-only BERT baseline (R²=0.439), with further improvement through hybrid co-training (R²=0.538).
AI.motivation: Molecular property prediction traditionally uses a single representative conformation, ignoring that molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. The authors aim to incorporate thermodynamic ensemble information into property prediction.
AI.method: EnsembleEGNN encodes each conformer with shared EGNN layers, pools representations via Set Attention Block, and is pretrained on CREMP cyclic peptide dataset using multi-task self-supervised objectives (masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, pairwise distance reconstruction).
AI.result: Scratch training fails (R²=0.005). Pretrained model achieves R²=0.477, Pearson r=0.699, outperforming BERT baseline (R²=0.439, r=0.667). Hybrid co-training with BERT further improves to R²=0.538, r=0.737.
AI.conclusion: Encoding conformational ensembles into thermodynamically informed embeddings significantly improves cyclic-peptide property prediction, demonstrating the value of ensemble-aware molecular representations.
